lead: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind, PMM-1, is a claimed device that creates energy. It either gives net work in a complete cycle with no energy input, or gives more work than the heat supplied to it, an efficiency above 100 percent. The first law forbids both, because energy is conserved. Only a few syllabi list PMM-1 as a separate topic; most teach it in a line beside the first-law statement. Engineers use the idea to reject impossible energy claims with one cycle balance, before any money is spent.
prereq: You need the cycle form of the first law, ∮δQ = ∮δW.

sections.h3: The two claims and the cycle balance

blocks.where: for any cycle: the net heat added (kJ) equals the net work done by the system (kJ), because the system returns to its starting state and ΔU = 0.

blocks.text: A PMM-1 claim comes in two forms. Form 1: a machine runs in a cycle, exchanges no heat and still gives net work. Form 2: an engine gives more net work W<sub>net</sub> than the heat Q<sub>in</sub> supplied to it. The cycle balance rejects both. With Q<sub>net</sub> = 0 it gives W<sub>net</sub> = 0, so a no-heat cycle cannot deliver work. And since W<sub>net</sub> = Q<sub>net</sub> = Q<sub>in</sub> − Q<sub>out</sub> with Q<sub>out</sub> ≥ 0, the work can never exceed Q<sub>in</sub>.
The converse statement is often quoted too: there can be no machine that delivers work continuously without some other form of energy disappearing at the same time.

sections.h3: Efficiency, and how to test a claim

blocks.text: η is the thermal efficiency (a pure number, often given in percent); W<sub>net</sub> is the net work out per cycle, Q<sub>in</sub> the heat supplied and Q<sub>out</sub> the heat rejected, all in the same unit.
Since Q<sub>out</sub> ≥ 0, η ≤ 1. A claimed efficiency of 125 percent means 125 kJ of work for every 100 kJ of heat supplied; the extra 25 kJ, a quarter of the input, would be created from nothing.

items: Put every energy flow on one basis: all in kJ per cycle, or all in kW.
Find Q<sub>in</sub>, Q<sub>out</sub> and W<sub>net</sub> from the claim.
If W<sub>net</sub> > Q<sub>in</sub> − Q<sub>out</sub>, energy is created: the claim is a PMM-1.
If W<sub>net</sub> is less than Q<sub>in</sub>, that alone is not a violation: the rest is heat rejected, which every real engine has.

blocks.text: A perpetual motion machine of the second kind, PMM-2, is different. It conserves energy but turns all the heat from a single reservoir into work. The first law cannot reject it; the second law does (see Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements).

figure.caption: The three claims of the worked example as energy bars. In (a) and (b) the work bar is longer than the heat bar, by 200 kW and 50 kW (outlined), so energy would be created. In (c) 60 kW of work plus 20 kW rejected equals the 80 kW supplied, so the first law is satisfied.

spec.aria: Three pairs of horizontal bars. Claim a: heat in 300 kW, work out 500 kW, the extra 200 kW outlined. Claim b: heat in 200 kW, work out 250 kW, extra 50 kW outlined. Engine c: heat in 80 kW, work 60 kW plus 20 kW of heat rejected, which balances.

examples.question: Test three claimed cyclic engines. (a) Takes in 300 kW of heat, delivers 500 kW of shaft work and exchanges nothing else. (b) Takes in 200 kW of heat and delivers 250 kW of work. (c) Takes in 80 kW of heat, rejects 20 kW to a river and delivers 60 kW of work.
steps: (a) Q<sub>net</sub> = 300 kW and W<sub>net</sub> = 500 kW. The cycle balance needs W<sub>net</sub> = Q<sub>net</sub>; the excess 500 − 300 = 200 kW would be created. PMM-1, impossible.
(b) η = W<sub>net</sub>/Q<sub>in</sub> = 250/200 = 1.25, that is 125 percent. Even with Q<sub>out</sub> = 0 the work can be at most 200 kW; 50 kW would be created. PMM-1, impossible.
(c) Q<sub>net</sub> = 80 − 20 = 60 kW = W<sub>net</sub>. The balance closes, so the first law is satisfied.
For (c), η = 60/80 = 0.75, or 75 percent. Whether 75 percent is reachable between the source and river temperatures is a second-law question, not a first-law one.
examples.answer: Claims (a) and (b) create 200 kW and 50 kW and are PMM-1; claim (c) satisfies the first law with η = 75 percent.

traps: Calling a low-efficiency engine a PMM-1. Low efficiency means heat rejected, not energy created.
Using Q<sub>in</sub> where the balance needs Q<sub>net</sub>: an engine that takes 80 kW and rejects 20 kW has Q<sub>net</sub> = 60 kW.
Confusing PMM-1 with PMM-2. PMM-1 breaks the first law; PMM-2 obeys it and breaks the second.
Mixing kW with kJ per cycle in one balance. kW is a rate; convert to one basis first.

quiz.a: A device that in a cycle gives net work with no energy input, or more work than the heat supplied (η > 100 percent).

quiz.q: Why does ∮δQ = ∮δW forbid a work-producing cycle with no heat exchange?
quiz.a: With Q<sub>net</sub> = 0 the balance gives W<sub>net</sub> = 0, so no net work can be delivered.

quiz.q: Give one line that separates PMM-1 from PMM-2.
quiz.a: PMM-1 breaks the first law by creating energy; PMM-2 conserves energy but breaks the second law by turning all heat from one reservoir into work.

quiz.q: A cycle takes in 80 kW of heat, rejects 20 kW and gives 60 kW of work. Is it a PMM-1?
quiz.a: Q<sub>net</sub> = 80 − 20 = 60 kW = W<sub>net</sub>; the balance holds, so it is not a PMM-1.

quiz.q: In a complete cycle Q<sub>net</sub> = 0. What is W<sub>net</sub>?
A claim has Q<sub>in</sub> = 400 kW and η = 110 percent. Find W<sub>net</sub> and decide.
quiz.a: W<sub>net</sub> = 1.10 × 400 = 440 kW. It exceeds Q<sub>in</sub> by 40 kW, which would be created, so the claim is a PMM-1.

beyond: Patent examiners see perpetual-motion applications every year and ask for a working model or an energy balance before going further. The same check runs in energy audits, where measured heat and work must close to within instrument error, and in process-simulation software, which flags any unit whose energy balance does not close. Search for “perpetual motion patent” and “energy balance closure” to see the rule in use.
